subject: 07D20A3AD4B944BD8CF60BEE1C34CE61
introduction: “Look not at your own capacities, for the divine bestowal can transform a drop into an ocean.” ‘Abdu’l-Bahá said this, in one form or another, to nearly everyone who protested that they were not fit to teach; the guide gathers some thirty instances, with Shoghi Effendi’s practical version: if the friends waited until they were qualified, nothing would be done. Scripture’s call stories all contain the same exchange, Moses’s “I am not eloquent”, Jeremiah’s “I am a child”, Gideon’s “my family is poor”, Isaiah’s “unclean lips”, each answered with “I will be with thee”; and Paul states the principle, “my strength is made perfect in weakness”. The Delphic “know thyself”, Paul’s “think soberly”, Emerson’s self-reliance and the parable of counting the cost ask whether ignoring one’s capacity is always wise.
questions: Why do the prophets’ call stories so often begin with a protest of unfitness? What does the answer “I will be with thee” change?
The readings say not to look at one’s capacity; Socrates says to know oneself. Can both be followed?
Reading 29 says waiting to be qualified would stop all work. In what kinds of service is that true, and where is preparation owed?
What is the difference between humility and the self-doubt these readings want removed?

outside.why: Let none consider the largeness or smallness of the receptacle. The widow’s oil flowed as long as there were vessels: there is not a vessel more. And the oil stayed.
Unworthiness does not shut one out. God be merciful to me a sinner; this man went down to his house justified.
Do not take your own capacity into consideration. O my Lord, I am not eloquent. And the Lord said unto him, Who hath made man’s mouth?
Ah, Lord God! behold, I cannot speak: for I am a child. But the Lord said unto me, Say not, I am a child.
Fix the gaze on the bounties of God. Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God.
The divine bestowal can make a tiny seed a lofty tree. The least of all seeds, when it is grown, becometh a tree.
Earth is barren until the rain. The desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose.
It is the strength of the Spirit that gives the power to teach. My strength is made perfect in weakness.
How often has one unlettered soul guided a world. They perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, and marvelled.
Look not at thy capacity. Gideon: my family is poor in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father’s house. And the Lord said unto him, Surely I will be with thee.
He will change the drop into an ocean. I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.
While teaching, turn to the Kingdom and seek confirmation. Take no thought how or what ye shall speak: for it shall be given you in that same hour.
None can deter thee. I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to gainsay.
Heed not your weaknesses; has He not in past days raised the weak? David to the giant: thou comest to me with a sword; but I come to thee in the name of the Lord of hosts.
God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty.
Ask not if you are worthy of the task. Woe is me! for I am a man of unclean lips. And his lips were touched with a coal from the altar.
“You must not say that you are dust.” We have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us.

Looking at our failures makes us despondent and frustrates effort. Paul asks for accurate self-assessment: not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think soberly. Is it possible to disregard one’s limits, as the readings ask, and still think soberly?
Socrates: I must first know myself, as the Delphian inscription says. The readings say, do not look at yourself. Are they answering a different question?

Never look at your own limitations. Emerson’s cure for self-doubt was the self: trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string. The readings’ cure is to look away from the self. Which have you found works?
The essential is to persevere and not be deterred. The servant with one talent was afraid, and went and hid it in the earth.
If the friends waited until fully qualified, the work would stand still. He that observeth the wind shall not sow; and he that regardeth the clouds shall not reap.
Jesus also said to count the cost before building a tower, lest one begin and be unable to finish. When is reading 29’s boldness right, and when the parable’s caution?
Do not be discouraged if the fruit is small. I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase.
The work done is not lost, however small its visible result. Whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.

shortfall: Readings 10 to 12, 15, 18, 19, 22, 23, 26 and 27 say “look not at thy capacity” in nearly the same words as their neighbours.

judges-my-family-is-poor.text: And he said unto him, Oh my Lord, wherewith shall I save Israel? behold, my family is poor in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house. And the Lord said unto him, Surely I will be with thee, and thou shalt smite the Midianites as one man
